message.content:
**1. DEMONSTRATED.** An omission one could and should have performed is attributable to the agent just as an act is, so it belongs to what one's hand has wrought.

**2. DEMONSTRATED.** "Remaining turned away" names a continuing state, and that state can hold from the first moment of knowledge without any prior facing.

**3. CONTESTED.** It is unsettled whether knowing only *that* a work is one's own suffices for culpable aversion, or whether knowing *what* it is is also required.

**4. DEMONSTRATED.** One can know one spoke a word or made a choice while its harmful consequences remain unseen.

**5. DEMONSTRATED.** If complete knowledge were required, no finite agent could face any work, since a work's consequences ramify without limit; facing it for what it is as far as known must suffice.

**6. DEMONSTRATED.** One can disown or flee one's good works through false humility, fear, or evasion of responsibility, so facing applies to goods as well as wrongs.

**7. FALSE AS STATED.** Taken universally, it fails: some works are irreparable or leave the right response genuinely unclear, as when the person wronged is dead.

**8. DEMONSTRATED.** Requiring every permissible deed could demand incompatible actions, so the obligation must be disjunctive.

**9. CONTESTED.** Attention can clearly occur without acknowledgment, but whether acknowledgment is itself a special kind of attention, attention to the work *as one's own*, remains open.

**10. DEMONSTRATED.** Even when the rightful deed is attention, such as attending to the one harmed, that is distinct from owning the work, so acknowledgment is still required in addition.

**11. DEMONSTRATED.** Facing is a sustained stance rather than a single event, and relapse into aversion after genuine turning is possible and common.

**12. CONTESTED.** Whether sorrow and resolve belong to the contrary of sin or are only its accompaniments depends on disputed accounts of what that contrary is.

**13. CONTESTED.** The compatibility of a received facing with the agent's ownership of it is the long-disputed question of grace and freedom.

**14. CONTESTED.** If grace names only a turning back, it presupposes prior aversion; if it can be given at the first moment of knowledge, it need not.
message.reasoning:
I'm working from a framing that defines sin as staying turned away from one's own work after knowing better, with repentance and grace as its opposite. I don't have the source text, so I'll judge each claim on general grounds and sort them into DEMONSTRATED, CONTESTED, or FALSE AS STATED, one line each.

I'm checking the remaining claims one at a time: omissions look attributable since they're things one could have done, so that one holds as demonstrated. Turning away from work never faced also seems demonstrated, because avoidance doesn't require prior facing. Whether someone can be faulted for not facing work whose nature they don't know is less clear, so I'm marking that one contested. Knowing something is yours while its consequences stay hidden still counts as demonstrated, since you can say something without realizing it caused harm.

I'm going through claims 5 to 9 now. Claim 5 looks demonstrated, since if facing something required knowing all its consequences, no finite agent could face anything at all. Claim 6 also seems demonstrated, because people do turn away from their good works through false modesty or disowning them. Claims 7 and 8 are less settled: whether a claim is determinate enough to guide action is often unclear, so I'm marking 7 contested, while 8 likely holds because the obligation is disjunctive rather than requiring every deed. Claim 9 I'm leaning toward contesting, since the "never" is a strong word to carry.

I'm weighing claim 9 against the idea that attention and acknowledgment might be the same thing. Close attention to one's own deed can happen while still disowning it or calling it someone else's, so acknowledgment seems to go beyond attention. That makes me lean toward marking 9 demonstrated, though some would argue acknowledgment is just attention under the right description, so it stays open.

Next I'm checking claims 9 through 13. I'm leaning toward marking 9 contested, since acknowledgment might just be attention under the right description, though attending to one's work as a spectator shows the two can come apart. Claim 10 seems demonstrated anyway, because attending to a victim is a different thing from acknowledging one's own work. Claim 11 holds, since repentance can arrive and then lapse, and "remaining turned away" implies a duration. Claims 12 and 13 look contested, as the role of sorrow, resolve, and grace in facing is unsettled.

I'm weighing whether claim 14 holds, since grace might name a turning back that presumes prior turning away, which would make the claim false as stated, but without the text I'm leaning toward contesting it. Claim 7 also needs a second look, because the "determinate enough to guide" wording may be the one that is false as stated rather than merely contested.

I'm settling claim 7 as false as stated, since what can rightly be done is often indeterminate, as when the victim is dead and the harm can't be repaired, so a universal claim of determinacy has counterexamples. I'm keeping claim 9 contested, because the strong "never" is hard to defend.
